# Question 1

Below, I simulate a rather quite annoying set of regression data.

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(0510)
n <- 250
dat.q1 <- tibble(x1 = rnorm(n, mean = 50, sd = 10),
                 x2 = factor(sample(c("A", "B"), n, replace = TRUE)),
                 x3 = factor(sample(c("Control", "Treat"), n, replace = TRUE)),
                 x4 = factor(sample(c("Low", "High"), n, replace = TRUE), levels=c("Low", "High")),
                 x5 = rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1),
                 x6 = factor(sample(c("Group1", "Group2"), n, replace = TRUE)),
                 x7 = rnorm(n, mean = 10, sd = 2),
                 x8 = rnorm(n, mean = 10, sd = 2)) |>
        mutate(y = 5 +                          # Intercept
                   # Quantiative x1
                   2 * x1 +
                   # Categorical x2
                   (x2 == "B") * 10 +
                   # Categorical x Categorical (x3*x4)
                   (x3 == "Treat") * 5 + (x4 == "High") * 2 + 
                   (x3 == "Treat" & x4 == "High") * 15 +
                   # Quantitative x Categorical  (x5*x6)
                   3 * x5 + (x6 == "Group2") * 4 + 
                   (x5 * (x6 == "Group2")) * 8 + 
                   # Quantitative x Quantitative (x7*x8)
                   1.5 * x7 + 0.5 * x8 + 
                   0.8 * (x7 * x8) + 
                   # Error
                   rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 15))
```
:::


 \normalsize

## Part a

Fit the regression model.

\begin{align*}
  Y_i =& \beta_0  +
       \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 I(x_{2i}=\text{B})+ \beta_3 I(x_{3i}=\text{Treat}) + \beta_4 I(x_{4i}=\text{High}) +\\
       & \beta_5 x_{5i} + \beta_6 I( x_{6i}=\text{Group2}) + \beta_7 x_{7i} + \beta_8 x_{8i}+\\
       & \beta_9 (I(x_{3i}=\text{Treat}) ~\times~ I(x_{4i}=\text{High})) + \tag{Categorical $\times$ Categorical}\\
        & \beta_{10} (x_{5i} ~\times~ I(x_{6i}=\text{Group2})) +\tag{Continuous $\times$ Categorical}\\
        & \beta_{11} (x_{7i} ~\times~ x_{8i}) +
         \epsilon_i \tag{Continuous $\times$ Continuous}
\end{align*}

**Solution:** First, we fit the regression model using `lm()`.

 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mod.q1 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3*x4 + x5*x6 + x7*x8, data=dat.q1)
```
:::


 \normalsize

As shown in the residual scott plot in  @fig-q1-residuals, the residuals appear uniformly distributed around 0, with both a highly positive and negative outlier preent. The distribution of the residuals in the quantile plot indicates approximate normality. With respect to the outliers, as shown in @fig-q1-outliers, while there are a few high leverage points and unusual points, the cooks distance and DFFITs plots suggest that they are not problematic for the regression.

## Part c
Interpret the intercept, the coefficients on $x_1$ and $x_2$.

**Solution**

The intercept $\beta_0$, is the expectation of $Y$ in the absence of any other continuous or categorical features of the model. Thus it's what the model expects of $Y$ if all continuous variables ($x_1,x_5,x_7,x_8$) are $0$, and all of the categorical variables $(x_2,x_4,x_6)$ are $0$, meaning that the observation is not in any of the categories. The coefficient $\beta_1$ indicates the increase in the expectation of $Y$ for a per unit increase in $x_1$, while the coefficient $\beta_2$ is the increase in expectation of $Y$ due to membership in category B.

## Part d
Untangle and interpret the $x_3*x_4$ interaction using algebra. Use @tbl-q1d-emmeans and @fig-q1d-emmeans for context.


 \scriptsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}

emm.q1d <- emmeans(mod.q1, ~x3*x4) |> # Don't average across levels: use |x2*x6
            data.frame() |>
            rename("Mean"  = "emmean",
```

```{.r .cell-code}
  mutate(Observation = paste("(x3=", x3, ", ", "x4=", x4, ")", sep=""))
ggplot(emm.q1d) + 
  geom_point(aes(x=Mean, y=Observation))+
```

:::
:::


 \normalsize

**Solution**
Given the interaction $x_3 \times x_4$, given this is a categorical x categorical interaction, we consider the state of the model under all combinations of values for $I(x_{3i} == Treat), I(x_{4i} == High)$

* **(Control, low)**
\begin{align*}
  Y_i =& \beta_0  +
       \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 I(x_{2i}=\text{B})+ \\
       & \beta_5 x_{5i} + \beta_6 I( x_{6i}=\text{Group2}) + \beta_7 x_{7i} + \beta_8 x_{8i}+\\
        & \beta_{10} (x_{5i} ~\times~ I(x_{6i}=\text{Group2}))\\
        & \beta_{11} (x_{7i} ~\times~ x_{8i}) + \epsilon_i 
\end{align*}
* **(Treat, low)**
\begin{align*}
  Y_i =& \beta_0  +
       \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 I(x_{2i}=\text{B})+ \\ &\beta_3 +\\
       & \beta_5 x_{5i} + \beta_6 I( x_{6i}=\text{Group2}) + \beta_7 x_{7i} + \beta_8 x_{8i}+\\
        & \beta_{10} (x_{5i} ~\times~ I(x_{6i}=\text{Group2})) +\\
        & \beta_{11} (x_{7i} ~\times~ x_{8i}) + \epsilon_i 
\end{align*}
* **(Control, High)**

\begin{align*}
  Y_i =& \beta_0  +
       \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 I(x_{2i}=\text{B})+ \\  &\beta_4 +\\
       & \beta_5 x_{5i} + \beta_6 I( x_{6i}=\text{Group2}) + \beta_7 x_{7i} + \beta_8 x_{8i}+\\
        & \beta_{10} (x_{5i} ~\times~ I(x_{6i}=\text{Group2})) +\\
        & \beta_{11} (x_{7i} ~\times~ x_{8i}) + \epsilon_i 
\end{align*}

* **(Treat, High)**
\begin{align*}
  Y_i =& \beta_0  +
       \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 I(x_{2i}=\text{B})+ \\ & \beta_3 + \beta_4  +\\
       & \beta_5 x_{5i} + \beta_6 I( x_{6i}=\text{Group2}) + \beta_7 x_{7i} + \beta_8 x_{8i}+\\
       & \beta_9 + \\
        &\beta_{10} (x_{5i} ~\times~ I(x_{6i}=\text{Group2})) +\\
        & \beta_{11} (x_{7i} ~\times~ x_{8i}) + \epsilon_i
\end{align*}

Using the values in the table:

* $\beta_3 = 219.4792 - 212.9676 = 6.5116$
* $\beta_4 = 216.4894 - 212.9676 = 3.5218$
* $\beta_9 = 238.1930 - 212.9676 - 3.5218 - 6.5116 = 15.192$
Thus, we interpret the total effect of $x_3, x_4$ to be $25.2254$, $6.5116$ due to membership in the treatment group, $3.5218$ due to membership in the high group, and $15.192$ the marginal increase due to membership in both groups.

**Solution**

the coefficient $\beta_{11}$ refers to the expected change in $Y$ for a unit increase in $x_{7i}$ after adjusting for the simultaneous linear change in $x_{8i}$ and vice versa.

\begin{align*}
\frac{\partial Y}{\partial x_{7i}} &= \beta_7 + \beta_{11}x_{8i} \\
\frac{\partial Y}{\partial x_{8i}} &= \beta_8 + \beta_{11}x_{7i}
\end{align*}


Since the slope of both variables is significantly positive for the entire range of observed variables and the lines are upward sloping, the interaction is positive and increasingly strong at higher values of both variables.

After standardization, a unit change represents a standard deviation change in the variable, simplifying the algebra:

* $z_{7i} = -1 \implies \beta_0 - \beta_7 + (\beta_8 - \beta_{11})z_{8i}$
* $z_{7i} = 0 \implies \beta_0 + (\beta_8)z_{8i}$
* $z_{7i} = 1 \implies \beta_0 + \beta_7 + (\beta_8 + \beta_{11})z_{8i}$

Thus, an increase of $1$ s.d of x_7 corresponds to an increase of $3.29$ in the slope of standardized $x_8$

# Question 2
@Cui25 investigate how freezing and cryogenic temperatures affect the strength, flexibility, stiffness, and internal breaking behavior of 3D-printed CF/PEEK composites.

Carbon fiber reinforced PEEK (CF/PEEK) is a high-performance composite used in 3D printing for aerospace, deep-sea, polar research. The researchers aimed to assess whether and how extremely cold environments impact this composite to understand how 3D-printed CF/PEEK performs in freezing conditions. This work would be important to understand its limits and develop preventative methods to protect against structural failures.

The researchers created fifteen 3D printed dog-bone-shaped test specimens and placed them in a chamber cooled with liquid nitrogen to $25^\circ\text{C}$, $-25^\circ\text{C}$, $-75^\circ\text{C}$, $-125^\circ\text{C}$, and $-175^\circ\text{C}$. To test strength of the specimen, a machine pulled both ends of the specimen until it snapped. 

In the table below, the researchers record the average tensile strength for three specimens from each temperature level.

| Temperature          | Mean Tensile Strength | 
| :--                  | :--                   |
| $25^\circ\text{C}$   | 81.93 MPa             |
| $-25^\circ\text{C}$  | 76.63 MPa             |
| $-75^\circ\text{C}$  | 63.23 MPa             |
| $-125^\circ\text{C}$ | 32.13 MPa             |
| $-175^\circ\text{C}$ | 12.83 MPa             |

## Part a
Compute the estimates we derived using calculus in lecture 16: 
\begin{align*} 
\widehat{\beta}_0 &= \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}_1 \\ 
\widehat{\beta}_1 &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{1i} - \bar{x}_1)(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{1i}-\bar{x}_1)^2}.
\end{align*}

**Solution**

$\overline{x} = -\frac{375}{5} = -75$

$\overline{y} = \frac{266.75}{5}=53.35$

\begin{equation}
\widehat{\beta}_1 = \frac{(25 + 75)(81.93-53.35) + (-25 + 75)(76.63 - 53.35) + (-75 + 75)(63.23 - 53.35) + (-125 + 75)(32.15 - 53.35) + (-175 + 75)(12.83 - 53.35)}{(25 + 75)^2 + (-25 + 75)^2 + (-75 + 75)^2 + (-125 + 75)^2 + (-175 + 75)^2} = .36536
\end{equation}

$\widehat{\beta}_0 = 53.35 - .36536(-75) = 80.752$

## Part c
Compute the maximum likelihood estimates using `optim()` in `R` as described in lecture 16:
$$\max_{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma\}).$$

**Solution**



 \normalsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
dat.q2 = tibble(
  temperatures =  c(25,-25,-75,-125,-175),
  measurements = c(81.93, 76.63, 63.23, 32.13, 12.83)
)

optim.func = function(params,data) {
  -1*sum(dnorm(data$measurements - (params[1] + (params[2] * data$temperatures)),0,sd=params[3],log=TRUE))
}

fitted = optim(
```

# Question 4

## Part a
Simulate data to match regression assumptions in a loop that runs $R=1000$ times.
\begin{align*}
    x_i &\sim \text{Uniform}(a=0,b=10)\\
    \epsilon_i &\sim \text{Gaussian}(\mu=0, \sigma=1)\\
    y_i &= 2 + 1.5 x_i + \epsilon_i\\
    n &= 30
\end{align*}
In each iteration, fit a regression line to the data and store the coefficient estimates. Plot the resulting estimates. What do you notice?

**Solution**

 \normalsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
regression.sims = function(r, n, error.dist) {
  beta0 = rep(0,times=r)
  beta1 = rep(0,times=r)
  for (i in 1:r) {
    dat = tibble(
      x = runif(n=n,min=0,max=10),
      e = error.dist(n),
      y = 2 + (1.5 * x) + e
    )
    mod = lm(y ~ x, data = dat)
    beta0[i] = coef(mod)[1]
    beta1[i] = coef(mod)[2]
  }

  list(
  tbl = regression.tbl(beta0,beta1),
  fig = regression.fig(beta0,beta1)
  )
 
}


regression.tbl = function(beta0,beta1) {
   tbl = tibble(beta0, beta1) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "parameter", values_to = "estimate") |>
    group_by(parameter) |>
    summarise(
      mean   = mean(estimate),
      sd     = sd(estimate),
      median = median(estimate),
      skew = e1071::skewness(estimate),
      kurtosis = e1071::kurtosis(estimate),
    ) |>
    knitr::kable(digits=2)
}


regression.fig = function(beta0,beta1) {
 pvt = tibble(beta0, beta1) |>
    pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "parameter", values_to = "estimate")
 
 plt = ggplot(pvt, aes(x = estimate)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "grey70", color = "white") +
    geom_vline(
      data = pvt |> group_by(parameter) |> summarise(mean = mean(estimate)),
      aes(xintercept = mean),
      color = "blue"
    ) +
    facet_wrap(~ parameter, scales = "free") +
    labs(x = "Estimate", y = "Count") +
    theme_bw()
}
```
:::


 \normalsize

 \normalsize


::: {#tbl-normsims .cell tbl-cap='Summary Statistics of Beta Coefficients with Normal Error'}

```{.r .cell-code}
out = regression.sims(r=1000,n=30, error.dist= \(n) rnorm(n))
(out$tbl)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

|beta1     |  1.5| 0.06|    1.5|  0.01|      0.0|


:::
:::


 \normalsize

 \normalsize


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
(out$fig)
```

The estimates for both coefficients are centered at the true values and normally distributed. The coefficient of variation of $\beta_0$ appears to be noticably larger than for $\beta_1$.

The estimates are no longer centered, and the coefficient of variation and skew are now sufficiently large such that the means cannot be reasonably interpreted to be representative of the population. Also, the incredibly high kurtosis indicates fatter tails, with a greater likelihood for outliers. This would explain the distortion in the x-axis in @fig-cauchysims. Taken together, the simulation suggests standard OLS is not appropriate for models with an error term sampled from a cauchy distribution with the given parameters.
